column1: # Every claim this product makes, the test that establishes it, and what it does NOT cover. Checked in BOTH directions by
#   * a claim naming a test that does not exist is a claim with no evidence
#   * a test no claim references is either an undocumented guarantee or a test that establishes nothing anyone cares about
# The second direction is the one that finds things. It is easy to write a document listing the claims you remember; it is
# hard to notice the guarantee you verify and never state, and that asymmetry is exactly where a safety argument goes
# wrong. An assessor reads this file, picks a row, and runs the test.
# Columns are tab-separated: ID, TEST, CLAIM, LIMIT.
# TEST is a ctest name, or NONE for a claim deliberately carrying no test (which must then be stated as unproven).

column3: CLAIM
column4: LIMIT

column3: The grounded extension is computed correctly, matching a reference implementation over generated frameworks.
column4: The reference is also mine, so this alone means consistent rather than correct. ENG-7 is the independent evidence.

column3: quorum's grounded labelling is confirmed EXHAUSTIVELY by CaDiCaL, which rebuilds the whole labelling from the identity that the grounded extension is the intersection of all complete extensions. All 50,688 states of four casebooks, 2,253,824 SAT calls, 0 mismatches. A self-test corrupts one label per casebook and requires the run to fail.
column4: CI gate (tools/cross-verify-exhaustive.sh); needs a CaDiCaL build, so it is not a ctest. The SAT encoding is mine; the SEARCH is Armin Biere's and shares no code with quorum.

column3: Work is bounded by 2n+2m steps in every framework tested.
column4: A bound on STEPS, not on time. Cycles need silicon.

column3: The emitted witness step bound is never exceeded: 2,195,456 reconstructions, zero truncations.
column4: Exhaustive for the casebooks tested, not a proof for arbitrary casebooks.

column3: All five Verdict outcomes are reachable, including Faulted, and each is reached by an adversarial fixture rather than by construction.
column4: Says the outcomes work, not that a given casebook produces the right one.

column3: A rejected add_attack is sticky: an incomplete casebook cannot finalize and produce a confident verdict.
When no fallback action exists, an invalid action index is returned rather than a plausible one.
The binding layer converts physical signals to propositions using integer arithmetic only, with 293 checks over thresholds, hysteresis, staleness and flatline.
column4: Hysteresis and staleness are modelled; sensor physics is not.

column4: One accident, reconstructed from a public report with the outcome known in advance.

column3: A stale channel does not repeat its last known value as though current, and losing one channel does not blind the device to others.
The compiler reproduces a hand-written casebook exactly: 16,384 states, 0 action differences, 0 outcome differences.
Non-interference and crash-resistance hold across a merged pump+tank palette over all 2^25 = 33,554,432 states: 0 label differences, 0 verdict differences.
column4: Two casebooks. Not a proof for arbitrary palettes.

column3: A combined palette header produces verdicts identical to the separate casebooks across 131,072 state pairs.
Realistic authoring mistakes produce actionable diagnostics that name the offending line.
column4: Only the mistakes its developers thought to make.

column3: Deliberately broken casebooks are refused with an actionable message rather than compiled into something plausible.
`vote k of` is exactly its hand-written expansion: 512 states, 0 outcome differences, 0 action differences.
A claim that cannot reach any action is reported, so logic that looks live and is inert does not pass review silently.

column4: Detects corruption and editing. NOT a security measure; it cannot resist forgery.

column3: The parser and lowering passes are tested independently of any casebook, including inputs that must be refused.
column4: A compiler that only works on the files we happen to have is not a compiler; these are the cases I thought to write.

column4: Fixed attacks only. Closed-world edges depend on the cycle's readings and cannot be represented in a static file.

column4: Compared at the one state a static file can describe (everything asserted, no closed-world edge live). Verifies the bridge to independent verification; nobody has crossed it.

The hand-written pump casebook produces the recorded verdict in each named diagnostic scenario.

column3: A witness renders the derivation in the author's vocabulary, using external one-based numbering and never internal indices.
column4: Readability is asserted by me, not tested on a reliability engineer.

column3: An FMEA table can be imported into a casebook draft, and the draft is REFUSED until a human supplies defeaters -- with the report saying that nothing in it is defeasible.
column4: The importer extracts what the table states. It cannot infer defeaters, because an FMEA does not record them; that is the engineer's contribution and the reason the draft is refused rather than compiled.

column3: hazop2cb reads an IEC 61882 worksheet, deduplicates deviations into observations, and reports two things from the Safeguards column: deviations with no protection, and deviations whose safeguard names the same instrument as the cause. It stays silent on a worksheet whose safeguards ARE independent, and the resulting draft is refused by cbc.
column4: LIMIT: the common-cause detector is instrument-TAG matching. It finds LT-101 in both columns; it cannot find a shared power supply, I/O card, control logic or calibration. Severities, defeaters and actions are TODOs because a HAZOP records none of them.

column3: The remedy suggested for a SHARED CAUSE is measured rather than asserted: the split casebook trips in 3 of 8 states, the merged one in 1 of 8. Pins the numbers the report quotes, so the advice cannot drift from the engine's behaviour.
column4: LIMIT: a 3-observation probe, not a plant. It establishes the DIRECTION of the tradeoff, not its magnitude on any real casebook.

column3: hazop2cb reports a SHARED CAUSE: one component failure written up under several deviations, which a row-by-row import silently turns into several unrelated claims. Found in a published hospital-oxygen HAZOP; the fix is to merge them into one claim needing the deviations together, making corroboration from independent parameters explicit.
column4: LIMIT: matches on cause text with filler words dropped and the rest sorted, so it catches rewordings but not synonyms or a different description of the same physical fault. It reports and explicitly REFUSES to prescribe a fix: merging measured 3-of-8 trip states down to 1-of-8, so the obvious remedy makes the safety function act less often. The report states the tradeoff instead.

column3: hazop2cb classifies safeguards by KIND (human inspection, procedure, the failing device's own alarm, tagged instrument) and reports two things the tag matcher cannot see: a SHARED LAYER carrying most of the document, and rows that are NOT AN IPL under CCPS criteria. Verified against a published hospital-oxygen HAZOP (PLOS ONE 2023, CC BY) where 13 of 14 rows are not an IPL.
column4: LIMIT: keyword classification, so it sees the phrasings listed in classify_safeguards and misses synonyms. The 2/3 shared-layer threshold is a stated judgement call, not a standard. Silence is not evidence of independence.

column3: Severity as ASPIC+ preference is load-bearing and conservative: a severity-2 rebuttal against a severity-9 claim is cancelled and the safe action holds in 2 of 4 states; at equal severity the rebuttal stands and it holds in only 1 of 4. Dropping the weaker attack makes the safety function act MORE often.
column4: LIMIT: a 4-state probe establishing the direction and the mechanism, not the magnitude on any real casebook. Severity values themselves remain an author's judgement that no tool can check.

column3: fmea2cb audits the scored half of an FMEA: it recomputes RPN from S x O x D, computes Action Priority from the AIAG & VDA 2019 lookup tables, and reports a RANK INVERSION where RPN ranks a row above one the standard ranks higher. In the shipped fixture a fuel union weeping (RPN 162, AP MEDIUM) outranks an airbag squib failing to fire in a crash (RPN 80, AP HIGH), and an RPN >= 100 threshold of the kind used in published studies would have discarded the airbag row entirely.
column4: LIMIT: whether an S, O or D rating is RIGHT is the team's judgement and cannot be audited. CONSTRUCTED fixtures, unlike the HAZOP and LOPA ones: both real FMEAs found are CC BY-NC-ND and cannot be shipped. See DOC-A19.

column3: A Detection column holding ratings is audited AND refused a casebook -- the ratings are exactly what the arithmetic needs and cannot become observations, because a reading called '7' is not one anyone can take. An Action Priority HIGH row with no recommended action is reported with its RPN shown, and a LOW row with no action stays silent.
column4: LIMIT: with --report the exit status reports the audit succeeding; without it the refusal is the whole result and the exit status is a failure. An FMEA has no Safeguards column, so none of the protection-layer questions can be asked of it at all.

column3: hazop2cb --report writes a review of a HAZOP with the same contract as the LOPA one: a SHA-256 that matches sha256sum, every finding located to a row with the document's own words quoted, what would settle each, all eight checks named including the silent ones, and its limits stated. On the hospital oxygen study it credits 14 of 14 rows for recording protection while reporting that none of it is an instrument.
column4: LIMIT: the report says what would SETTLE a question, never what to decide. A HAZOP has no arithmetic, so no finding can ever appear under 'the document contradicts itself'.

column3: The CAPECO row is reported as both UNPROTECTED and COMMON CAUSE with the shared tag lt-101 quoted from the document, and the unprotected finding is presented as the study's own conclusion rather than as a contradiction in it -- because a cell reading 'None' is what the document says, not an error in it.
column4: LIMIT: this reads the words in a cell. A safeguard named there may be uncalibrated, bypassed, or wired to a failed I/O card, and the worksheet would look identical.

column3: lopa2cb --report writes a review a customer can act on: provenance with a SHA-256 that matches sha256sum, every finding located to a line of their worksheet with its own words quoted, what would settle each one, and a reproduction command that runs. Findings are recorded once as structured data and rendered twice, so the report cannot silently disagree with the terminal output.
column4: LIMIT: the report states what would SETTLE a question, never what the engineer should decide. The file is not byte-identical run to run because it embeds the output path it was given; the findings are.

column3: The report names every check that ran, including the ones that found nothing, and states what was not checked at all. On the biocontainment study four of seven checks are listed as silent; on a clean study all seven are, with zero findings and the limits still stated. A correct document is presented as correct -- 4 of 4 rows confirmed -- and never filed under 'the document contradicts itself'.
column4: LIMIT: naming a silent check proves it ran, not that it would have fired on a defect; that is what the mutation tests are for.

column3: The SHA-256 used to tie a report to a document revision matches FIPS 180-4 for the empty input, a single block, and a 56-byte input that forces a second padding block, and agrees with an independent implementation on a real file. Deleting the second padding block fails the test.
column4: LIMIT: used for identification, not security. There is no adversary constructing a colliding HAZOP.

column3: lopa2cb audits a Layer of Protection Analysis against its own stated arithmetic. On the published biocontainment study (Harsono et al., Sci Rep 15:4428, 2025, CC BY) it independently reproduces the paper's conclusions exactly -- total mitigated frequency 1.4e-05/yr, required PFD 7.14e-02, SIL 1 -- and reports NO arithmetic defect, while naming two protection layers whose independence from their initiating cause the document does not establish.
column4: LIMIT: the arithmetic tolerance is a factor of two, because LOPA is semi-quantitative and rounding to one significant figure is the method working as intended. Independence findings are candidates, not verdicts: a layer may name a system and still be wired independently of it, and the document's silence is the finding.

column3: lopa2cb catches a wrong exponent in a row's own stated answer, a layer claiming more credit than IEC 61511 allows its kind, a conditional modifier counted among the protection layers, a layer credited against every initiating cause, and a study that states no target at all. It stays completely silent on a clean study built to approach every one of those boundaries without crossing it.
column4: LIMIT: the credit cap recognises control-system and human/procedural layers by keyword and exempts anything declaring a SIL. A layer whose kind is not named in its description is not capped, so silence is not evidence the credit is justified.

column3: hazop2cb reads the standard HAZOP worksheet, which has no Deviation column: a deviation is a guide word applied to a process parameter, so Guide Word and Parameter are combined into one deviation and announced. High and Low stay distinct observations. A Parameter column with no Guide Word is refused, because combining on the parameter alone was measured to collapse two 'Level' rows into a single observation carrying both causes.
column4: LIMIT: the combination is ordered guide-word-first ("High level") because that is how a team reads it aloud; a worksheet whose parameter already contains the sense ("Level high") will read slightly oddly but stays distinct. Guide words themselves are not validated against the IEC 61882 list.

column3: hazop2cb handles the shapes a real worksheet arrives in: it searches forward for the header past an Excel banner and reports how many rows it skipped, keeps reported line numbers matching the file, and detects a binary .xlsx/.xls/.pdf and says to export as CSV rather than quoting its bytes into an error.
column4: LIMIT: the header is recognised by containing a known word, searched at most 20 records in. A multi-row header parses but a Guide Word split across two header rows is silently dropped, which is recorded as still open in DOC-A8.

column3: hazop2cb reads RFC 4180 multi-line quoted cells, so a bulleted list inside one cell no longer shifts every column after it; reports PACKED CAUSES when one cell holds several causes; reads a second MITIGATIVE safeguards column so a preventive-only "None" is no longer a false UNPROTECTED; reports UNPROVEN LAYER where the document itself says a safeguard was never proof tested; carries a word-graded Severity column across as a suggestion; and refuses politely when a worksheet exceeds 30 deviations, explaining that a casebook covers one node.
column4: LIMIT: causes are split on newlines and semicolons only, never commas, because prose uses commas constantly. The severity word mapping is a defensible reading of a 5-point scale, not a standard, and is never written into the casebook.

column3: hazop2cb analyses German PAAG worksheets: Abweichung/Ursache/Auswirkung/Gegenmassnahmen columns, and German safeguard vocabulary so that "keine" is UNPROTECTED and "geraeteeigener Alarm" is the failing device's own alarm. The refusal message now lists every column name recognised and states plainly that only English and German are supported.
column4: LIMIT: English and German only, and the German vocabulary is what could be confirmed from sources rather than a complete lexicon. A worksheet in another language parses and reports every safeguard as unclassifiable -- honest, and useless.

column3: hazop2cb distinguishes DEFERRED safeguards ("TBD", "see note 4", "under review") and UNCLASSIFIED prose from real protection, instead of waving both through. Found by mutation testing: the Instrument classification was decorative, because a fallback gave unreadable text the same standing as a tagged trip -- so "See note 4" was reported as fully protected.
column4: LIMIT: keyword lists again. A deferral phrased outside the list still reads as unclassified, which is reported rather than assumed safe -- the failure direction is now conservative.

column3: The compiler's refusal limits are enforced and explain themselves: 31 observations is refused citing the 32-bit mask, and `vote 5 of` over ten transmitters (C(10,5)=252 branches) is refused past the 64 cap. Both gaps were found by mutation testing -- loosening either left all 43 tests green.
column4: LIMIT: covers the two limits mutation testing exposed. tools/mutate.py is not a CI gate because each mutation needs a rebuild and a full ctest run.

column3: A casebook that ignores `<channel>_unavailable` LOSES the safe action when the sensor dies mid-alarm: measured stop_transfer while healthy, carry_on once the latched channel goes stale. tank.cb, which does reason about it, holds stop_transfer across the same transition. Proves cbc's _unavailable warning corresponds to real lost safety rather than being advice.
column4: LIMIT: one channel, one threshold, one transition. It proves the warning is load-bearing, not that every casebook ignoring _unavailable fails in the same way.

column3: An action reachable by exactly ONE route is reported as a SOLE ROUTE with the observations it depends on, starred when it is the safe action. Found pump.cb's safe state reachable only via bearing_wear; silent on vote.cb, whose 2oo3 trip has three routes.
column4: LIMIT: reports, never refuses -- a single trip amplifier is often the legitimate protection. It says the route exists and is sole; whether that is acceptable is an engineering decision.

column3: For every action, cbc reports observations on which ALL routes depend -- a common-cause failure that defeats the whole protection. Implements CCPS Independent Protection Layer criterion 2. Found a real violation in pump.cb on first run: four diagnoses, one accelerometer.
column4: LIMIT: reports, never refuses -- a single switch is often a legitimate protection. Covers observation-level common cause via support edges only; it does not model shared power, shared I/O cards, shared control logic, or shared calibration, which are the common causes a real LOPA also considers.

column4: LIMIT: reports, never refuses -- a deliberate default-holding argument is the Piper Alpha pattern and legitimate. Detects a missing gate edge; it cannot tell a deliberate assumption from an accidental one.

column4: LIMIT: proves the gate reacts to four kinds of drift, not that those are the only kinds. A wrong number that is regenerated consistently from a wrong tool still passes.

column4: LIMIT: covers comma-grouped integers in README.md only. Small numbers, percentages, and prose claims elsewhere are not covered, and a wrong number that is merely PLAUSIBLE and consistently regenerated would still pass.

column4: The reads-high direction was missing until a mechanised single-symptom check found it. Thresholds and the proof-test response are engineering judgement.

A static worst-case bound of 2,571 instructions holds across every state of every casebook, derived from the Cortex-M33 disassembly by implicit path enumeration.
column4: Does NOT model the memory system. RP2350 runs from QSPI flash through a cache and a miss costs far more than an instruction.

column3: The cycle-counting harness is correct across both counter widths, including the 24-bit down-counting SysTick, and reports which counter it used.
column4: Tests the rig, not the timings.

column3: The staged tree survives a real vendor BSP, not only a stub: two identifier collisions with vendor macros were found and fixed (Source::SysTick against CMSIS, binding::bit() against the Arduino core), and the headers stage as an Arduino library because the Arduino build never puts the sketch folder on the include path.
column4: Backed by CI gate 15 (tools/arduino-portable-check.sh), not a ctest, because it needs Docker. LIMIT: gate 15 still compiles against a stub Arduino.h, which proves self-containment and cannot prove survival of a real BSP. Only running a vendor toolchain does that, and only for the vendor tried.

column3: Measured execution time on real silicon, on the Cortex-M33 the bound was derived for and on a second vendor. Raspberry Pi Pico 2 (RP2350, Cortex-M33, 150 MHz), three runs, DWT CYCCNT, worst-case state: solve fastest 2,809 cycles every run, slowest 3,719 (24.8 us, 1.45 CPI against the 2,571-instruction bound, under the 2 CPI assumed; the bound converts to 34.3 us); worst full cycle 21,746 cycles (145.0 us) for the pump with a cold cache. A 16,384-state sweep on the silicon picked the same worst state as kWorstCaseMask. Arduino Uno R4 Minima (RA4M1, Cortex-M4, 48 MHz): solve 3,608 cycles (75.2 us, 1.40 CPI), full cycle 13,646 (284.3 us), min = max exactly, identical on two flashes. Both devices took exactly the 140 steps cbc predicted, inside the proven bound of 248. Raw captures: firmware/pico2/measured-2026-09-29.txt, firmware/arduino/measured-2026-09-29.txt.
column4: PROVEN AS A MEASUREMENT, NOT AS A WCET. On the cached RP2350 the slowest run moved between flashes (3,466 / 3,719 / 3,681) while the fastest did not, so a measured maximum there is evidence that the bound is not optimistic rather than a guarantee; the instruction bound is what is guaranteed, and its conversion to time rests on a CPI now measured at 1.40-1.45. The cache is not analysed statically. Margins on a 1 ms cycle: 6.9x worst full cycle on the Pico 2, 3.5x on the 48 MHz part, 29x for the solve bound alone.

column4: Gated by tools/footprint.sh in CI, not by ctest. Requires docker.

column3: A reliability engineer outside BioDream can encode a casebook from an FMEA and have the validator surface an ambiguity they did not know their document contained.
column4: UNPROVEN, and the most important missing evidence. All five casebooks were written by quorum's developers, from documents they chose, with outcomes they already knew.

column3: Limited temporal reasoning. A rulebook can say `X within T after Y`, `X within last T` and `X N times in T` (timed readings, TIME-1..5), chain them (a timed reading may watch another, with no loops), and hold a threshold `for T`; a timed reading cannot watch a conclusion, and nothing can be said about intervals the device did not see.
column4: Stated as a limit, not a claim. The rules are checked in every combination of readings; when a timed reading is set is checked by tests (TIME-1, TIME-3, TIME-4, TIME-5) and on each board, not by exhaustive validation, and never on a plant. Watching a conclusion is refused because the rules' answers would feed back into their inputs and exhaustive validation would no longer cover what the device does.

column3: Six pump misalignment and resonance states cannot be separated without a phase discriminator.
column4: A hardware limit, correctly surfaced as ambiguity rather than guessed.

column3: A casebook can be LEARNED from labelled cases, as AA-CBR (Cyras, Satoh & Toni 2016), and decided by quorum's own unmodified grounded solver. Every past case is an argument; a more specific case with the other outcome attacks a less specific one, subject to concision; the new case attacks every irrelevant case; the prediction is the default outcome iff the default is IN. Past-case attacks run strictly from more features to fewer, so the framework is acyclic and every labelling is total. Checked against an independent oracle that shares no code with the implementation, on every query of 400 random casebases (8,734 queries) under both coherence policies, and by 10 mutations of the attack conditions and the policy, all killed.
column4: LIMIT: binary outcomes and at most 32 binary features. HOST ONLY: learning allocates and has no WCET; the learned casebook is meant to be validated and compiled, never changed on a device. Vanilla AA-CBR assumes a coherent casebase; the majority-per-pattern repair is this implementation's choice, not the literature's, and is measured in LEARN-2.

column3: On real data -- UCI Congressional Voting Records, 435 rows, CC BY 4.0 -- majority-coherent AA-CBR with information-gain feature selection, k chosen by nested cross-validation inside each training fold, scores 95.63% (416/435) under 10-fold CV, against 95.63% for naive Bayes, 95.40% for 1-NN and 61.38% for the majority class. The learned frameworks are small: at most 5 arguments and 4 attacks per query. VANILLA AA-CBR is measured as well and FAILS on this data: at k = 2 it scores 39.77%, below the majority class, because after duplicates collapse one republican case overrules 245 democrats sharing its pattern.
column4: LIMIT: this dataset is dominated by one vote (physician fee freeze), and at the k nested CV picks, every method reduces to nearly the same one-feature rule -- so parity with naive Bayes shows the pipeline is sound, NOT that argumentation learns better. With all 32 features AA-CBR scores 81.38% against 93.10% for 1-NN, because a case is relevant only if the query has every one of its features. A dataset where the methods diverge is needed before any claim of advantage. The ctest asserts only total labellings, solves within bound, and beating the majority class.

column3: On a dataset where no single feature decides -- UCI Tic-Tac-Toe Endgame, 958 boards, 27 binary features, CC BY 4.0 -- AA-CBR with information-gain selection and k chosen by nested cross-validation scores 84.03% (vanilla) and 82.99% (majority-coherent) under 10-fold CV, against 98.64% for 1-NN, 69.83% for naive Bayes and 65.34% for the majority class. Every labelling total, every solve inside its proven bound. So AA-CBR learns something real here -- 14 to 19 points over naive Bayes -- and is decisively beaten by nearest-neighbour.
column4: LIMIT: the comparison does NOT favour argumentation on accuracy, on either dataset tried. With all 27 features AA-CBR equals the majority class exactly, structurally: every board sets exactly nine features, so no case is ever a strict subset of another and none is ever relevant. The majority-coherence repair does not help here (25 disagreements favour vanilla, 14 favour the repair, sign test p = 0.108). An author-chosen encoding using only the nine "x in cell i" features reaches 92.48% against 97.08% for 1-NN; it is excluded from the result because it was chosen knowing the concept. The frameworks are larger than a shipped casebook: up to 476 arguments and 1,241 attacks per query at the selected k.

column3: Thresholds can be learned from data rather than written: Fayyad & Irani (1993) MDL discretisation, with no parameter to tune, finds the cut between separable classes at the midpoint, both boundaries of a two-sided rare-failure band to within 5 of the truth on 9,000 records, every true boundary and no extra one when uncapped, and NO cut on labels that are independent of the signal. A marginal cut that pays for log2(N-1)/N but not for the Delta term is rejected, as the paper requires. 5 mutations, all killed.
column4: LIMIT: one signal at a time, binary outcome. The number of cuts per signal is capped (2 in use) for the 30-observation device limit, and under the cap cuts are taken best-first rather than by full recursion, a stated departure from the paper. HOST ONLY: the learned thresholds are an input to a casebook, not something a device learns.

column3: Pre-registered test v2 (learn/PREREGISTRATION.md) on UCI AI4I 2020, reproduced byte for byte: with learned thresholds, adding learning to each of the 6 incomplete casebooks raised balanced accuracy in 6/6, by +19.87 points on average (registered bar +10). In counts, the incomplete casebooks alone missed 1,131 failures and with learning 320, for 78 false alarms among 57,966 normal records. The registered VERDICT is NOT SHOWN: criterion 2 (the casebook improves learning at n = 500) won 5/6, missing by one failure.
column4: LIMIT: v2 is a SECOND look at the same data, designed after v1 failed (v1: +8.37, 5/6), and is weaker evidence for it. Across five further shuffle seeds criterion 1 held every time (+17.2 to +19.9) and criterion 2 in three of five. AI4I is synthetic, with documented generating rules. About 55 of the 339 failures are random modes no method predicts. Checked only on GCC 9 / x86-64, the toolchain that made the record: the experiment uses standard-library shuffling and distributions, which libstdc++ implements differently in later versions (see the portable re-run, LEARN-13 to LEARN-15).

column3: Pre-registered replication v3 on the MONK problems, data not used in any design, reproduced byte for byte: it FAILED all three accuracy criteria. Learning raised an incomplete casebook to 100% in two of four conditions (83.33 to 100, 57.89 to 100) and tied or lost in the other two, and with the complete, correct MONK-3 casebook it made 12 new mistakes from 6 mislabelled training records. Two defects found and recorded: noisy records manufacturing exceptions to correct rules, and false alarms when what is missing cannot be expressed in the available observations.
column4: LIMIT: the claim is that the replication was run as registered and failed, and why. Four conditions only; MONK-2 excluded for a stated reason. Checked only on GCC 9 / x86-64, the toolchain that made the record: the experiment uses standard-library shuffling and distributions, which libstdc++ implements differently in later versions (see the portable re-run, LEARN-13 to LEARN-15).

column3: Pre-registered test v4 on 200 freshly generated problems, with both v3 defects repaired (an exception to a reviewed rule needs 2 supporting records; the learner may choose to learn nothing), reproduced byte for byte. Against the incomplete casebook, learning won 148, tied 47 and lost 5, a mean gain of +18.41 points. The guard worked: with the complete casebook the repaired method stayed within 1 point on 196/200 problems against 167/200 unrepaired. The registered VERDICT is NOT SHOWN: 148/200 is 74%, under the registered 80%, and the gain over learning alone was +4.41, under the registered +5.
column4: LIMIT: the problems come from a generator written for this test (3-term DNF over one-hot attributes), which is the regime AA-CBR represents well; nothing here measures real-world concepts. 14 of the 47 ties are problems where the missing knowledge was redundant. The casebook contribution to learning fades with data (+1.79 and +2.92 at n = 200). Checked only on GCC 9 / x86-64, the toolchain that made the record: the experiment uses standard-library shuffling and distributions, which libstdc++ implements differently in later versions (see the portable re-run, LEARN-13 to LEARN-15).

column3: A learned model compiles as an ordinary casebook with nothing lost or added: the learner writes .cb source (claims, excuses, rebuttals, a when-any action), the same parse/lower/check passes as for a hand-written casebook accept it, and the compiled framework decides EVERY one of the 2^observations states exactly as the learner predicts, for six learned casebooks (MONK-1 and MONK-3, three starting casebooks each; 1,504 states in all). Cases with no path of attacks to the default (spikes; Paulino-Passos & Toni 2021) are pruned before emission, 78 of 108 learned cases here, and the every-state check runs after pruning. Each case is written as the right kind (claim or excuse). 5 emitter mutations, all killed.
column4: LIMIT: equivalence is to the learner, not to the truth: a wrong model compiles into an equally wrong casebook. No exclusive groups are emitted for one-hot encodings, deliberately, because cbc would add instrument-fault doubts the learner never had. Observations only: learned thresholds are not yet emitted as channel declarations.

column3: The cbc binary itself, full validation pass, accepts the two learned casebooks that contain learned exceptions (5 of 12 and 2 of 3 claims defeatable): every state Decided, no state selects two actions, every solve inside its 2n+2m bound, every declared action reachable.
column4: LIMIT: two casebooks. Acceptance means the casebook is well-formed and bounded, not that it is accurate.

column3: cbc REFUSES the four learned casebooks that are pure rule lists, for exactly one reason: nothing in them can be argued against, so they are decision trees and do not need an argumentation engine. Three are the casebook alone, because the learner chose to learn nothing; one added rules but no exceptions. The compiler was not weakened to admit learned input; the check asserts the refusal and that it is the only failure.
column4: LIMIT: this is the compiler policy for FMEA imports applied unchanged to learned ones. Whether a learned rule list should ship anyway, as a plain rule list, is a product decision not made here.

column3: The device header cbc emits for a learned casebook (MONK-1, 45 arguments, 98 attacks, 10 observations) decides all 1,024 states exactly as the learner did, compared by a per-state fingerprint (FNV-1a, 795 assertions), and its worst solve is 167 steps against a proven bound of 306. Runs on every build: the learner writes the casebook at build time, cbc compiles it, the host runs the header.
column4: LIMIT: the ctest runs on the HOST CPU. The same header was run on silicon on 2026-10-01 and printed the identical line on both boards, Pico 2 (Cortex-M33, 150 MHz) and Uno R4 (Cortex-M4, 48 MHz), with 167 steps, inside the bound, and no state undecided; raw captures in firmware/pico2/measured-learned-2026-10-01.txt and firmware/arduino/measured-learned-2026-10-01.txt. Those are one run each, not a ctest.

column3: The data image cbc --blob writes for centrifugal-pump loads in the device loader and decides EVERY state identically to the compiled header from the same source: same outcome, same action, same step count. column3: qblob, using the device loader itself, sweeps the pump image through the runtime path with every solve inside the proven bound (140 of 248 steps), and prints the DEVICE line the board must print. On 2026-10-01 a studio-made image on a Pico 2 printed it exactly: 16,384 states, fnv1a 0xe5408b85, worst cold 25,727 cycles = 171.513 us at 150 MHz.
column4: LIMIT: the silicon results are single runs, not ctests. 171.513 us is about 18% above the compiled-header build of the same casebook because of the larger fixed capacity. The same image built for an Uno R4 Minima (Cortex-M4, 48 MHz) printed the identical DEVICE line, worst cold 18,240 cycles = 380.000 us; and on that board a one-bit corruption was refused as damaged (CRC) and two swapped attack targets with a repaired CRC were refused as a fingerprint mismatch, neither deciding (firmware/arduino/measured-runtime-2026-10-01.txt). The Pico 2 refusal run was lost when the board dropped off USB.

column3: learn2cb drafts a casebook from a plain records table with no hand-written code. On AI4I 2020 it skips the row ID and the product code, flags the four failure-mode columns (TWF, HDF, PWF, OSF) as recorded after the event because the outcome follows each in every record that has it, and with them left out drafts a casebook that cbc validates over all 1,024 states, reporting a 5-fold cross-validated balanced accuracy against the majority class.
column4: LIMIT: AI4I is synthetic. The cross-validated estimate is on the records given and says nothing about a machine. Leak detection is a heuristic (one column alone explains 90% of the outcome entropy, or 98% of its records are positive); it cannot find a leak spread over several columns. The learning stage benefit remains NOT SHOWN in the pre-registered tests.

column3: A palette image (cbc --palette --blob; pump and tank on one device) loads in the palette loader and decides as the compiled palette header from the same cbc run: same edges, member slices, closed worlds and names, and for each member every one of its states, with the other member at 10 settings (none, all, 8 pseudo-random), gives the same outcome, action and step count for BOTH members' policies, 491,520 combined states in all, each inside the proven bound. A flipped byte and two swapped attack targets with the CRC repaired are refused; the single-casebook loader refuses a palette as an unknown format.
column4: LIMIT: host CPU, and a sample of the 2^29 combined states, not all of them; the palette's non-interference argument (cbc validate_palette, test_palette's 33.5 million state cross-product) is what covers the rest. A palette has no binding layer: like the palette header it takes the presence mask directly, so it cannot tell a dead sensor from a quiet one.

column3: Swept through the runtime path with the other member quiet, each palette member prints exactly the DEVICE line of its casebook alone (pump fnv1a 0xe5408b85, tank 0x90bc4385). On 2026-10-01 an Uno R4 Minima running the studio-made palette image printed both lines exactly, every solve inside the bound of 484 steps, worst cold 31,288 cycles = 651.833 us (firmware/arduino/measured-palette-2026-10-01.txt).
column4: LIMIT: one run on each board. On 2026-10-05 a Pico 2 printed both lines exactly too, worst cold 35,338 cycles = 235.586 us at 150 MHz, and refused a one-bit-flipped image (image damaged (CRC)) and an image with two attack targets swapped and its CRC repaired (fingerprint mismatch) (firmware/pico2/measured-palette-2026-10-05.txt). Each member's step count includes the other member's arguments, because the combined framework is solved once.

column3: cbc --symbolic labels every argument and decides every state at once (BDDs), and agrees with the device solver (solver::Grounded + arbiter::decide) on every label and outcome in every state of every shipped casebook. On the pump + tank palette it covers all 536,870,912 combined states and proves each member's decision depends on no other member's readings.
column4: It computes no per-state step counts, so device images still need the exhaustive validation. BDD size depends on variable order and is not bounded in general. The palette's agreement with the device solver is checked on a sample of 5,127 states, not all of them; the non-interference result itself is exact.

column3: A proof certificate (cbc --certificate) can be checked by tools/qcert, about 200 lines of C99 sharing no code with quorum, and every minimal forgery tried is rejected: a flipped label, a moved round, a changed outcome or action, a deleted or duplicated state, a redirected attack, a changed fallback or idle action, a nudged setpoint (where there are thresholds), truncation, and a wrong device fingerprint. Pump: 16,384 states.
column4: qcert checks that the certificate is internally consistent and matches the fingerprint, not that the rulebook is right. qcert hashes the setpoints without judging them. The forgeries tried are the ones listed, not all possible ones. The checker is also mine.

column4: Format 3 is written only when a hold exists; that images without holds stayed byte-identical to the previous cbc was checked once by hand, not by a test. Since 2026-10-11 the fingerprint covers setpoints and holds, and every runtime_blob_* test requires an image with an edited setpoint or fallback (CRC repaired) to be refused.

column3: The AI guard never lets a proposal make the outcome less cautious than the rulebook's: over every state and every possible proposal of the pump (49,152 pairs), 46,326 accepted, 2,826 replaced, 0 weaker. Each guard reason is reached on a hand-built ranking. The same line is reproduced on the Uno R4 and the Pico 2.
column4: Cautious means as cautious as the rulebook's `prefer` order. The guard makes the combination no less cautious than the rulebook; it does not make the proposing controller safe, and it cannot correct a wrong rulebook or faked inputs.

column3: As GUARD-1 for tank-409: 131,072 pairs, 41,728 accepted, 89,344 replaced, 0 weaker. The test reports that the safe action does NOT outrank every other action here: `stop_and_evacuate` outranks `stop_transfer`, so the guard accepts stop-and-evacuate where the rulebook says stop.
column4: That the higher action includes the stop rests on its name and description, which a person approves; the guard checks only the ranking.

column3: A PLC can drive quorum over Modbus RTU (functions 03, 06 and 16) and get exactly the decision it would get directly: all 16,384 pump states through the registers agree (MODBUS line 0x074d5609, reproduced on the Uno R4 and the Pico 2). The guard works through the registers. Raw channel samples go through the binding with holds and staleness. Bad CRCs are dropped silently, broadcasts are not answered, and every exception code is produced.
column4: Modbus has no authentication: anything on the link can choose quorum's inputs (runtime/GUARD_AND_MODBUS.md). Tested over USB serial only, not RS-485. This is a host test of the slave core; the silicon runs are measurement files, not ctests.

column3: The portable re-run of v2 (PREREGISTRATION.md, 2026-10-06; same data, seeds, method and criteria, random choices drawn compiler-independently) is reproduced byte for byte, and gives the same output on GCC 9 and GCC 14 (x86-64) and GCC 14 on a Raspberry Pi 5. Criterion 1 6/6, +19.75; criterion 2 6/6, +15.65; no harm; verdict YES.
column4: LIMIT: NOT a new test and NOT evidence that v2 passes: the registered v2 result is NOT SHOWN. This is one more shuffle of the same data; criterion 2 was already known to hold on some shuffles and not others (three of five further seeds), and the verdict flips on it.

column3: The portable re-run of v3 is reproduced byte for byte and is identical on GCC 9, GCC 14 and the Pi 5. Criteria 1 and 2 still FAIL (2/4, +13.77; 2/4, +7.83); criterion 3 (no harm with the complete casebook) passes on this draw; verdict NOT SHOWN.
column4: LIMIT: one more draw of v3's inner folds, not a new test. The criterion-3 flip shows how much 122 training rows leave to chance; the registered v3 result, criterion 3 FAIL, stands.

column3: The portable re-run of v4 (200 problems drawn afresh from the same generator and seed) is reproduced byte for byte and is identical on GCC 9, GCC 14 and the Pi 5: learning beats the incomplete casebook on 157/200 (+18.83), beats learning alone on 104/200 (+3.75), within 1 point of the complete casebook on 195/200; verdict NOT SHOWN, as registered.
column4: LIMIT: a different set of 200 problems from the registered v4, so it is a second sample of the same generator, not a replication on new kinds of problem.

column3: Exhaustive validation runs on every hardware thread and its output does not depend on how many: the report, the device header and the chip image are byte-identical with 1, 3 and 16 threads (18-reading rulebook, 262,144 states).
column4: LIMIT: compares cbc with itself across thread counts. That the threaded walk equals the previous single-threaded cbc was checked once (2026-10-14, every repository rulebook, 60 runs), not on every build.

column3: cbc --commissioning writes the loop-check sheet for the pump: the fingerprint the board reports, the device's action order, the action at rest, and one row per reading with the action alone and the fewest other readings with which it changes the decision.
column4: LIMIT: the sheet states what the rules do. Whether the plant feeds them the right readings is shown only by a person working through it on the real machine, which no plant has done.

column3: A second implementation of the language (tools/refcheck.py), written from the documentation and evaluating the rulebook text directly, decides every state of every repository rulebook and of 300 random rulebooks exactly as cbc does; six deliberate mistakes in it are each noticed.
column4: LIMIT: written by the same developer, from documentation the same developer wrote, so a shared misreading of the language is less likely but not excluded. Random rulebooks cover claims, excuses, doubts, the four kinds of evidence, attacks, severity, implies and exclusive; not channels or timing.

column3: Timed readings (`reading ... when X within T after Y`, `within last T`, `N times in T`) are set exactly as LANGUAGE.md defines them: each kind at its window boundary (inclusive), order respected, a held relay counted once, the 32-bit millisecond wrap crossed, an event a full clock turn (49.7 days) old not mistaken for a recent one, chains (a timer watching an earlier timer, stepped in table order) worked by hand, and every unusable table refused at configure time, including one that watches a later timer or loops. 360,000 timer-steps over random histories, half of them from tables with chains up to three deep, agree with a second implementation that keeps the whole history and applies the definitions literally; a deliberately planted off-by-one window, a broken edge detector and a chain that ignores the earlier timer were each caught.
column4: LIMIT: written by the same developer as the device code. Edges are seen only when the device steps, so a source that is set and cleared between two steps is missed; the runtime steps about every millisecond. Never run on a plant.

column3: A rulebook with timed readings compiles to a format-4 image that the device loader reads back identical to the compiled header (every timer field), and both decide all 512 states of the fixture alike. A lengthened timer window with a repaired CRC is refused as a fingerprint mismatch, an unconfigurable timer table is refused at load, and a timed image relabelled as format 3 does not load. Rulebooks without timed readings produce byte-identical headers, images, certificates and fingerprints (the whole suite was unchanged).
column4: LIMIT: one fixture rulebook, written to exercise all three kinds.

column3: Over Modbus, the timed fixture behaves as written while only the clock and the written readings change: pressure 4.9 s after a start stops the pump and 30 s after alarms; an overheat is remembered for exactly 5 minutes from when it was last SEEN, through tick() alone; three overload trips within an hour lock out until an hour after the first; a master writing a timed reading's bit does not set it; and readings written set and cleared within the same millisecond, with no read or tick between, still count (three trips lock out, an overheat is remembered). The test clock (registers 10-12) cannot be turned on without the key, inside a longer write, or once a controller has written; it cannot move half a number or more than 24 days at once; and it crosses each window exactly to the millisecond.
column4: LIMIT: host-run, with a simulated clock. On a Pico 2 and an Uno R4, each with its own clock (firmware/*/measured-timed-2026-10-26.txt, single captures, not under CI), 8 of 8 timed checks passed on each, including three trips seen only between requests; the 5-minute and 1-hour expiries were not waited for there.

column3: The bench script cbc writes for the timed fixture (each timed reading just inside and just outside its window, then every line of the commissioning sheet) is played against the device's own Modbus map on its test clock, and all 19 answers agree. The script's answers come from replaying the whole script through the definitions over the full history, not from the device's timer code; a script with one answer changed is caught.
column4: LIMIT: host-run. On a Pico 2 (firmware/pico2/measured-bench-timed-2026-10-26.txt, single captures, not under CI) the studio's bench test passed 19 of 19 on the test clock and 19 of 19 in real time (71 minutes); the Uno R4 has not run it.

column3: As TIME-4, for a fixture with five timed readings declared out of order and chained three deep (a count of an `after` that watches a `within last`; a `within last` of a `within last`): 17 answers agree. Removing the test clock's stops at each expiry inside a jump is caught.
column4: LIMIT: as TIME-4, one fixture. A scene whose readings share inputs so that it cannot mean what its label says is left out of the bench test, with a note from cbc; the fixtures have none.

column3: As TIME-2, for the chained fixture: the format-4 image with five timers in dependency order loads identical to the header and decides all states alike.
column4: LIMIT: as TIME-2.

column4: LIMIT: host-run; lateness drawn from a fixed seed, uniform up to 50 ms. A bench later than that by more than the script's margins (100 ms to 5 s, by window) is not covered.
